session_title: Pre-Conference Online Tutorials
title: Deploying Research and Education Apps on ACCESS and NAIRR Resources with iDLab and OneSciencePlace
speakers: Amit Chourasia, Benjamin Winjum, Choonhan Youn, and Jerome Ronquillo
description: The NSF ACCESS and NAIRR ecosystems provide researchers and educators with access to advanced computing, data, and AI resources, yet many users still face practical barriers to using command-line workflows common on HPC and AI resources. This tutorial introduces iDLab, an NSF-funded effort to advance federated interactive computing and data environments, and OneSciencePlace, the composable platform that enables the creation of science gateways, HPC/AI portals, research applications, and data publication environments via a low-code/no-code interface. Participants will learn how OneSciencePlace enables applications to be deployed and accessed via a web browser by individual researchers, classrooms, research groups, campus programs, and broader consortia. The tutorial will focus on hands-on use and deployment of applications on selected ACCESS and NAIRR resources, aligning with iDLab's goal of making advanced computing and data resources easier to use across institutions. Examples will include AI inference and machine learning classification via interactive web applications such as Jupyter, interactive VNC applications such as Linux Desktop, and batch command-line applications on HPC systems. Participants will also review more complex application interfaces and create a simple app with a custom web form for parameters, inputs, and execution. This tutorial builds on two well-attended OneSciencePlace tutorials delivered at Gateways 2024 and Gateways 2025. It extends them by placing greater emphasis on deploying applications on ACCESS and NAIRR resources, introducing newer OneSciencePlace capabilities, and situating the work within the broader iDLab effort. By the end of the tutorial, attendees will understand how a single user-facing gateway can simplify access to distributed HPC and AI systems while supporting the reproducibility, provenance, reuse, and publication of computational applications. Project website: https://onescienceplace.org/

session_title: Pre-Conference Online Tutorials
title: AI-Native Science with Galaxy
speakers: Tyler Collins and Ahmed Awan
description: This tutorial introduces participants to the Galaxy Project, an open source platform designed to make computational research more accessible, reproducible, and transparent. After an overview of the platform's interface and core design goals, participants will work through a complete, hands-on metagenomic analysis — used here as a vehicle to examine how AI capabilities, both built into Galaxy and integrated from external sources, can be applied within a real-world analysis. Additionally, we will also have a discussion of their current capabilities and limitations. Designed for a mixed audience of developers, scientists, and educators, the session assumes no prior experience with Galaxy. Through a short lecture and guided exercises, participants will explore workflow construction, tool access, and reproducibility practices, as well as practical ways to incorporate AI assistance into their research. By the end of the 90-minute session, participants will have hands-on experience running a metagenomic analysis on Galaxy and a grounded understanding of how AI tools can support real-world computational research workflows in Galaxy, as well as where their current limitations lie.

session_title: Pre-Conference Online Tutorials
title: Designing Frequently Asked Questions and Knowledge Bases for Science Gateways: Tutorial on Question Design, Help Architecture, and AI-Ready Documentation
speakers: Noreen Whysel, Shari Thurow, and Bev Corwin
description: Effective user support documentation, including frequently asked questions (FAQs) and structured knowledge bases, is a recognized and important component of usable, sustainable Science Gateway infrastructure. Complex, collaborative environments like Science Gateways require structured support documentation to improve usability and discoverability, particularly as access to these systems is increasingly mediated by artificial intelligence (AI). The authors audited Science Gateway websites listed in the Science Gateways Community Institute (SGCI) catalog and found that 92% do not provide an FAQ or structured self-service help documentation. This gap directly limits researchers' self-sufficiency and AImediated access to gateway resources. This tutorial addresses that gap via information architecture (IA) principles, humancentered design methods, and emerging human-centered artificial intelligence (HAI) heuristics. A human-in-the-loop approach to FAQ curation and maintenance anchors these methods, ensuring that both human users and large language model (LLM)-powered interfaces can locate, access, and accurately interpret help content. These methods apply to both new and existing Science Gateway help systems. Attendees will examine three FAQ and knowledge base design patterns and apply question-generation strategies grounded in both human expertise and AI. Participants leave with an FAQ design checklist and wireframe templates with specifications, all immediately applicable to improving usability, findability, and accessibility in their own gateway environments. This tutorial is intended for Science Gateway researchers, developers, and educators seeking to improve researcher self-sufficiency and ensure help content is accurately found and interpreted by both human users and AI-powered interfaces.

session_title: Pre-Conference Online Tutorials
title: Integrating Data Tools and Interactives with Open Educational Resources: From Creation to Publishing to Teaching
speakers: Drew LaMar, Sam Donovan, and Deborah Rook
description: Science gateways can achieve broader impacts through the creation of teaching materials, like Open Educational Resources (OER), that utilize their gateway's scientific data and computational tools. However, many educators and researchers remain unsure how to create, enrich, and publish them effectively. This hands-on tutorial guides participants through the full OER lifecycle, from authoring and interactive tool development to publishing and classroom integration. Participants will be introduced to the landscape of education gateways and OER authoring platforms, including Gala, PreTeXt, and Quarto, before diving into practical experience creating their own learning module using Quarto on Posit Cloud. The tutorial then explores how data tools, such as Observable and Jupyter Notebooks, and modern WebAssembly-based technologies, such as Quarto Live and Shinylive, can transform static content into dynamic, interactive learning experiences. The final portion of the tutorial covers publishing workflows, as well as strategies for effectively deploying OERs in teaching contexts. By the end of the session, participants will leave with a clear pathway for developing and sharing OERs within their own gateway communities.

session_title: Pre-Conference Online Tutorials
title: Building AI-Enabled Gateways for Data Publication, Discovery, and Analysis with Globus
speakers: Vas Vasiliadis and Lee Liming
description: Motivated by the growing data sharing and collaboration needs in the research enterprise, we will describe how Globus services may be used to dramatically increase the value of research products. In this tutorial we will demonstrate how to easily generate and deploy a data portal—without hosting infrastructure—and automatically generate and ingest metadata into a search index, enabling data publication that meets FAIRness mandates while ensuring compliance with security and privacy regimes. We will then evolve the portal to a science gateway by adding remote computation via functions-as-a-service (FaaS), making the data reusable by collaborators. Finally, we will introduce the Globus Model Context Protocol (MCP) server and demonstrate how complex remote computation tasks can be delegated to AI agents, allowing the research pipeline to scale without human effort.

session_title: Pre-Conference Online Tutorials
title: Looping the AI Lifecycle: Automated Training and LLM-Driven Evaluation via Tapis v3 & NAIRR Vista
speakers: Anagha Jamthe, Wei Zhang, Joe Stubbs, Nathan Freeman, and Christian Garcia
description:
This tutorial provides researchers with a comprehensive, hands-on introduction to advanced, reproducible Machine Learning (ML) workflows using the production-grade services of the Tapis v3 platform. Focusing on the complete machine learning engineering pipeline, participants will learn how to "loop" the AI lifecycle by orchestrating automated model training and executing sophisticated, LLM-driven evaluations directly on distributed computational resources. Through practical, step-by-step exercises, we will demonstrate how to seamlessly manage infrastructure using the Tapis Application Programming Interface (API) and the intuitive Tapis User Interface (UI). The session will deeply emphasize the integration of various Tapis core capabilities alongside specialized services, specifically launching Tapis jobs for automated training and FlexServ for LLM inferencing to build distributed reproducible scientific AI workflows. By the end of this tutorial, researchers and engineers will be fully empowered to efficiently develop, deploy, evaluate, and maintain automated AI lifecycles within their own research paradigms.

Attendee Preparation: To participate in the hands-on portions of the tutorial, attendees should create and activate a TACC account in advance by visiting [here](https://accounts.tacc.utexas.edu/register).

session_title: Session 1: Platforms, Portals and Federation
title: Building a Portal for the NAIRR Pilot Project
speakers: Jeanette Sperhac, David Benham, Ilya Shunko, Jesse Woo, Sandra Gesing
description: **Session Moderator:** Sabrina Perry, Austin Peay State University
abstract: This paper outlines considerations for building a web portal for the NSF's National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR) Pilot project. The NAIRR Pilot seeks to support and advance academic AI development and use in the US. Accordingly, the portal team equipped an AI-focused science gateway with custom components such as interactive sandboxes, dynamic project statistics, and a user assistance chatbot. The portal described here serves as the face for the NAIRR Pilot project.

session_title: Session 1: Platforms, Portals and Federation
title: Extending the TACC Core Portal Science Gateway to Support Multi-Institutional HPC with Tapis and TMS
speakers: Sal Tijerina, Joe Stubbs, Nathan Franklin, John Gentle, Frank Netscher, Steve Black, Dan Vernon, Sean Cleveland, Jake Rosenberg, Sophia Massie-Perez, Tracy Brown, Mayal Dahan
description: **Session Moderator:** Sabrina Perry, Austin Peay State University
abstract: Science gateways remain an essential component of research infrastructure and are a proven resource in lowering the barrier to entry for high performance computing. Many science gateways are built to be tightly coupled to a given research institution, resulting in varying experiences and tooling across computing centers. Since 2018, the Core Portal science gateway has been under continuous development as an open-source, domain-agnostic science gateway framework, built to be a responsive and efficient user interface with a robust feature set aimed at improving the experience and capabilities of conducting HPC research through a web interface. Powered by the Tapis API middleware - developed at the Texas Advanced Computing Center (TACC) - to interface programmatically with HPC resources, the Core Portal provides a unified, feature-consistent web interface for data management, application code abstraction, job submission and monitoring, and static content management - enabling HPC access across a wide variety of scientific domains without requiring terminal commands or complex authentication workflows. Recently, the Core Portal has expanded its capabilities to support institutions external to TACC, with users authenticating through Tapis via CILogon through InCommon-federated identity providers, currently supporting several external institutions. The Trust Manager System (TMS) developed at TACC addresses the core challenge of credential management by enabling seamless, no-human-in-the-loop MFA, while the forthcoming Tapis Resource Providers API will allow registered institutions to define available resources, enabling the Core Portal to automatically discover and configure access based on institutional affiliation, advancing toward a universal science gateway experience.

session_title: Session 1: Platforms, Portals and Federation
title: iDLab: A Federated Browser-Based Platform for Interactive Computing and Data Across ACCESS and NAIRR Resources
speakers: Amit Chourasia, Amit Majumdar, Amiya Maji, Brett Bode, Joeseph Stubbs
description: **Session Moderator:** Sabrina Perry, Austin Peay State University
abstract: Researchers increasingly work across multiple high-performance computing (HPC), cloud, and data resources. Each system typically presents its own interface, authentication mechanism, software environment, and data management workflow. Learning and maintaining these differences is a recurring cost, and it falls hardest on new users, educators, students, and research communities without dedicated computational support. The Interactive Discovery Laboratory (iDLab) is developing a federated platform that provides a consistent browser-based experience for interactive computing, data access, and application delivery across geographically distributed cyberinfrastructure. iDLab is led by the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), in collaboration with the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA), the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center (PSC), Purdue University, the San Diego Supercomputer Center (SDSC), and the Texas Advanced Computing Center (TACC). It is built on the OneSciencePlace (OSP) platform, developed by UCLA, SDSC, and TACC, and targets resources within the Advanced Cyberinfrastructure Coordination Ecosystem: Services and Support (ACCESS) and the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR). This presentation describes the architecture and implementation of iDLab: identity federation, an application catalog, interactive and batch execution brokered through Tapis, and shared data access, presented through a single web interface. Interactive desktops, Jupyter notebooks, visualization tools, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning workloads, and traditional HPC jobs are discovered and launched through a common interface while executing on participating site resources. Applications are deployed and operated independently at each site. iDLab presents them consistently rather than replacing local software stacks, schedulers, storage systems, or operational policies. We describe the federation model under development with participating cyberinfrastructure providers, including approaches to identity federation, site-local application deployment, catalog metadata publication, and user experience consistency across independently operated resources. The design builds on existing site infrastructure and practices rather than requiring sites to adopt new ones. The talk closes with current integration status across participating sites and what we have found so far in multi-site identity federation, application deployment, and operational coordination. We identify open problems and invite collaboration with gateway developers, cyberinfrastructure providers, and research communities as iDLab moves toward pilot deployment. Project website: https://idlab.onescienceplace.org

session_title: Session 1: Platforms, Portals and Federation
title: UpStream: An Open, Reusable Science Gateway Service for Accessible, Discoverable Environmental Sensor Data
speakers: William Mobley, Suzanne A. Pierce, Kasey M. Faust, Daniel Butcher, Christian Garcia
description: **Session Moderator:** Sabrina Perry, Austin Peay State University
abstract: UpStream is a lightweight, open, and reusable science gateway service that leverages Tapis cyberinfrastructure, allowing domain scientists, not only computing specialists, to quickly establish sensor streams and transfer field observations into analysis-ready, discoverable data collections from remote field environments to managed TACC-hosted resources. UpStream addresses the sensing problem as a service providing data acquisition, API-first ingestion, campaign to measurement metadata data model, and browser-based visualization to support reliable access to environmental time-series data. This work lowers the setup barrier by leveraging the use of Tapis Pods, Actors, and a unified authentication and authorization. UpStream helps surface long-tail environmental data collections that would otherwise remain invisible on field loggers and individual machines, making them findable and reusable. We demonstrate the service with a representative deployment that connects tilt meters in remote, subarctic permafrost field sites in Alaska. Reliable, discoverable field data is a foundational input for downstream decision support and decision provenance. UpStream contributes a set of reusable design patterns for remote environmental sensing that decouples acquisition from gateway operations, pull-based incremental transfer, containerized portable ETL, and schema-on-ingest.

session_title: Session 1: Platforms, Portals and Federation
title: Supporting AI-Assisted UX Evaluation in Scientific Cyberinfrastructure: An Interaction-Profile Perspective
speakers: Paul Parsons, Hamed Abdulsalam, Phuong Bui
description: **Session Moderator:** Sabrina Perry, Austin Peay State University
abstract: Scientific cyberinfrastructure supports diverse forms of work, including computational workflows, data discovery, learning, collaboration, simulation, and decision making. As organizations begin exploring the use of AI to support UX evaluation, ensuring that AI-generated feedback remains grounded in the work a system is intended to support becomes an important challenge. Drawing on a corpus of more than 100 science gateways identified through UX consulting engagements and a public gateway catalog, we identify recurring interaction profiles that characterize common forms of work across gateway ecosystems. We then synthesize prior UX literature and practitioner experience to connect these profiles to recurring UX concerns and opportunities for AI-supported inquiry. Rather than treating gateways as a homogeneous category of systems, our interaction-profile perspective helps teams consider how different forms of work give rise to different evaluation needs. We argue that effective AI-assisted UX evaluation requires attention to the work users are trying to accomplish and offer interaction profiles as a practical means of providing that context.

session_title: Session 1: Platforms, Portals and Federation
title: How a Small Team Develops, Maintains, and Advances an Earth Systems Science Gateway
speakers: Ana Espinoza, Julien Chastang, Mohan Ramamurthy
description: **Session Moderator:** Sabrina Perry, Austin Peay State University
abstract: NSF Unidata is a program within the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR) that develops open source software for the distribution, analysis, and visualization of Earth system science (ESS) data. Students, educators, and researchers access data and computing resources on the NSF Jetstream2 (JS2) cloud through the Unidata Science Gateway. The gateway combines established Unidata technologies, including the Local Data Manager (LDM) for ingesting real-time data feeds and the Thematic Real-time Environmental Distributed Data Services (THREDDS) Data Server for serving those datasets through standards-based, interoperable, protocols such as HTTP(S), OPeNDAP, and WMS. These data are analyzed and visualized using applications including MetPy, the Advanced Weather Interactive Processing System Common AWIPS Visualization Environment (AWIPS CAVE), and the Unidata Integrated Data Viewer (IDV). Users access these capabilities through JupyterLab as part of a customized Python for Atmosphere and Ocean Science (PyAOS) JupyterHub deployment running on Kubernetes clusters provisioned through OpenStack Magnum on Jetstream2. The gateway integrates interactive scientific workflows with browser-based scientific desktop applications, including AWIPS CAVE and IDV, providing a complete cloud-native environment that eliminates the need for local software installation. We present several recent developments to the Unidata Science Gateway, including a customized PyAOS environment supporting the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) Cloud Model 1 (CM1) as an example of the platform's flexibility, and a new capability that enables IDV to use a large language model (LLM) for image-based analysis of atmospheric visualizations through a GPU-hosted vLLM inference service running on Jetstream2. We also describe how a two developer team leverages open source technologies to simplify gateway deployment and maintenance, improve security, and support reproducible scientific computing. These technologies include Nushell for infrastructure automation and configuration management, Image Builder for producing secure, up-to-date virtual machine images, nbgallery for sharing notebooks and scientific workflows, and conda-store for managing reproducible, shareable Conda environments. Together, these technologies enable a small development team to deliver secure, extensible, and reproducible science gateway services to the Earth system science community.

session_title: Session 2: Data Foundations: FAIR, Governed, Shared, Verifiable
title: Compliant Data Sharing and Collaboration with Globus
speakers: Vas Vasiliadis
description: **Session Moderator:** Sajida Faiyaz, Austin Community College
abstract: Science gateways and data portals are most valuable when the data they host can be easily shared across institutional boundaries and moved from institutional storage systems and shared facilities (campus clusters, core facilities, national labs, cloud platforms) to external collaborators and analysis environments. Ensuring that these data egress workflows are secure, compliant with institutional and regulatory policies, and repeatable is a major challenge for research computing, campus IT, and data stewards. This talk introduces attendees to Globus capabilities for secure, policy-aware data sharing and controlled data egress, with a particular focus on automation. We will describe how to: enable institutional storage for secure, compliant access via Globus; implement access control and sharing policies to enable secure data egress to external collaborators and environments (including cloud); and automate complex, multi-step data egress workflows using Globus Flows. The talk will survey the breadth of capabilities and controls available for data sharing and provide a concrete starting point for research computing professionals implementing data collaboration infrastructure that complies with institutional and regulatory policies.

session_title: Session 2: Data Foundations: FAIR, Governed, Shared, Verifiable
title: Digital Agriculture Sandbox for Collaborative Research
speakers: Osama Zafar, Rosemarie Santa Gonzalez, Alfonso Morales, Erman Ayday
description: **Session Moderator:** Sajida Faiyaz, Austin Community College
abstract: Digital agriculture is transforming the way we grow food by utilizing technology to make farming more efficient, sustainable, and productive. This modern approach to agriculture generates a wealth of valuable data that could help address global food challenges, but farmers are hesitant to share it due to privacy concerns. This limits the extent to which researchers can learn from this data to inform improvements in farming. This paper presents the Digital Agriculture Sandbox, a secure online platform that solves this problem. The platform enables farmers (with limited technical resources) and researchers to collaborate on analyzing farm data without exposing private information. We employ specialized techniques such as federated learning, differential privacy, and data analysis methods to safeguard the data while maintaining its utility for research purposes. The system enables farmers to identify similar farmers in a simplified manner without needing extensive technical knowledge or access to computational resources. Similarly, it enables researchers to learn from the data and build helpful tools without the sensitive information ever leaving the farmer's system. This creates a safe space where farmers feel comfortable sharing data, allowing researchers to make important discoveries. Our platform helps bridge the gap between maintaining farm data privacy and utilizing that data to address critical food and farming challenges worldwide.

session_title: Session 2: Data Foundations: FAIR, Governed, Shared, Verifiable
title: CloudSec: Cross-Layer Access Control Policy Analysis for Science Gateways
speakers: Mohamed Elrefaiy, Joe Stubbs
description: **Session Moderator:** Sajida Faiyaz, Austin Community College
abstract: On a science gateway, a researcher's intended access policy and the system's actual enforcement are expressed at different layers. The two are never compared. On Tapis-based gateways, the gap widens over time, as permission grants that each seem reasonable accumulate into access nobody intended. We present CloudSec, which extends the automated reasoning of Stubbs et al. (ACR'24) to cross-layer policy alignment. CloudSec models the intended policy U and the extracted system policy S as sets of (subject, resource, action) tuples, related by a mapping φ. Each divergence is then classified: a misconfiguration (D1), a concept discrepancy (D2), or unrealized intent (D3). CloudSec runs as a web application beside a gateway's Tapis tenant. Members sign in with their existing Tapis identity. A Python service pulls role hierarchies, resource shares, and permission grants from the Security Kernel over standard Tapis interfaces. The current implementation translates these into an Alloy model and checks it with the Alloy Analyzer. The interface reports a D1 violation as a counterexample naming a specific user, resource, and action, and shows it beside the model that was checked. From there, a finding traces back to the grant that produced it. The intended audience is a domain scientist, not a security specialist, so a large language model (LLM) fronts the interface. It turns a question in plain language into a structured plan naming the analysis to run and the user to examine. By design, the LLM only plans. It has no tools and cannot start an analysis; it can only propose one. Every plan passes server-side validation and an explicit human confirmation before anything runs. Today the intended policy U is a single fixed rule: a user may only read or change data they own. Eliciting U from the researcher's own words is the planned extension of this interface. We demonstrate the pipeline end-to-end on policy data from 3dem.org, a production cryo-electron microscopy gateway. Extraction replays a recorded snapshot of the gateway's security policy: the roles, permission grants, and shares as they stood at one moment. That keeps a run reproducible and cheap to repeat as a gateway evolves, and it lets a result be re-checked later against the same records. The talk walks through one run, from those records to the generated model and back to a verdict a gateway operator can read.

session_title: Session 2: Data Foundations: FAIR, Governed, Shared, Verifiable
title: Achieving FAIR Compliance in a Domain Science Gateway: Lessons Learned and Operational Experience from the C-MĀIKI v2 Migration
speakers: Andy Yu, Sean B. Cleveland, Craig E. Nelson, Nicole A. Hynson, Mahdi Belcaid, Kiana Frank, Nicole Yoneishi
description: **Session Moderator:** Sajida Faiyaz, Austin Community College
abstract: The C-MĀIKI science gateway version 2 emerged from two simultaneous pressures, a mandatory migration from the deprecated Tapis v2 (Agave) API to Tapis v3, and a user-driven requirement to adopt Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable (FAIR) data practices as the gateway's user base and interconnected dataset volume grew. This paper reports on the specific tooling built to address the metadata compliance requirement, a schema-driven Metadata Tool that guides researchers through standards-conformant entry using the MIxS standard and EMPO vocabulary, paired with a lightweight enforcement gate at job submission. We describe the design decisions behind this two-stage model, the operational lessons learned since deployment, and the guiding principle that compliance should be made as easy as possible by integrating it into the existing user workflow.

session_title: Session 2: Data Foundations: FAIR, Governed, Shared, Verifiable
title: OSC-IS: A Blockchain-Backed Science Gateway for Verifiable Research Artifact Preservation
speakers: Fernando Garzon
description: **Session Moderator:** Sajida Faiyaz, Austin Community College
abstract: Scientific research increasingly depends on digital artifacts such as datasets, source code, notebooks, models, configuration files, documentation, and analysis outputs. However, these artifacts are often distributed across personal drives, Git repositories, cloud buckets, institutional storage, and publication supplements, making long-term preservation, provenance tracking, and reproducibility difficult. OSC-IS is a science gateway prototype designed to provide researchers with a structured portal for storing, organizing, and verifying research artifacts through a combination of cloud infrastructure and blockchain-backed provenance. The OSC-IS portal allows researchers to upload and manage project artifacts through a web interface, preserving both the files and their associated metadata. The system is designed around a modern full-stack architecture that integrates an Angular frontend, a NestJS backend, PostgreSQL metadata storage, object storage for files, asynchronous processing through RabbitMQ, and Hyperledger Fabric smart contracts for tamper-evident artifact records. This architecture separates artifact storage from artifact verification: large files are stored in scalable cloud object storage, while blockchain transactions preserve verifiable metadata, provenance, and integrity references. This talk will present the motivation, architecture, implementation, and lessons learned from building OSC-IS as research cyberinfrastructure. The focus is not blockchain as a standalone technology, but its practical role in supporting trust, auditability, and reproducibility in a science gateway context. The presentation will discuss how the portal supports artifact submission, metadata capture, storage workflows, and verification mechanisms, as well as the engineering tradeoffs involved in combining web gateways, cloud-native services, and permissioned blockchain networks. OSC-IS is intended as a prototype platform for improving the preservation and validation of scientific artifacts across research communities. By providing a gateway-oriented interface over complex backend infrastructure, the project explores how researchers can interact with reproducibility and provenance tools without needing to understand the underlying blockchain or cloud architecture. The talk will also address future directions, including integration with institutional research workflows, improved researcher onboarding, persistent identifiers, access control, and broader support for reproducible computational research.

session_title: Session 2: Data Foundations: FAIR, Governed, Shared, Verifiable
title: Web-Based Processing of RAPID’s LA Wildfires Large Geospatial Dataset using DesignSafe’s Responsive, Unified Platform Hazmapper
speakers: Shayan Khan, Nathan Franklin, Sal Tijerina, John Gentle, Sophia Massie-Perez, Joseph Wartman, Jeffrey Berman, Karen Dedinsky, Michael Grilliot, Ellen Rathje
description: **Session Moderator:** Sajida Faiyaz, Austin Community College
abstract: Following the Palisades and Eaton wildfires that devastated communities near Los Angeles, California in January 2025, burning over 15,000 hectares, destroying more than 16,000 structures, and causing an estimated $100 billion in losses, Uncrewed Aerial Systems (UAS) and mobile street view imaging systems were deployed to document damage across both burn areas. These surveys produced 30 km² of near-centimeter-resolution orthomosaics, 3D point clouds, digital surface models (DSMs), and 640 km of ground-level street view imagery across the Palisades (6.5 km²) and Eaton (23.5 km²) fire areas. This high-resolution dataset was collected using the RAPID facility’s advanced instrumentation. Datasets of this scale and variety require specialized desktop GIS software, creating barriers for broader research and public access. HazMapper addresses this by incorporating server-side processing pipelines that convert data into web-friendly, cloud-native formats, enabling interactive browser-based exploration. In the Los Angeles Wildfire use case, HazMapper’s low-lift operational experience to examine these surveys served diverse users across research domains with both critical timing and in-depth insight into the impact of the fires concerning infrastructure, environmental factors, and public health. Surveys, conducted in February and March 2025, collected data via UAS flights and mobile street view imaging (SVI) systems. UAS imagery was processed with photogrammetry software to generate orthomosaics, DSMs, and point clouds, while street view imagery was uploaded to Mapillary. Initial processing was completed in the field or at the RAPID facility before the data was transferred to DesignSafe via Globus, resulting in 57.5 TB of data, after which 7.15 TB of data was published in a DesignSafe project and became publicly accessible. The data was then prepared for web visualization before it could be displayed in HazMapper. Orthomosaics were converted into Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs) using GDAL and served as map tiles via TiTiler. Point clouds were converted with PotreeConverter for interactive 3D visualization in Potree. The data was brought together in a HazMapper project, where users may examine orthomosaics, point clouds, and street-level imagery within an interactive map interface. While the data is currently accessible via ArcGIS tile services, the combination of COGs and TiTiler provides an open alternative served directly from DesignSafe storage resources. HazMapper enables these massive geospatial datasets to be openly accessible through its web interface, integrated within the DesignSafe science gateway specialized in supporting natural hazards research, allowing researchers to interactively explore orthomosaics, point clouds, and street view imagery (sourced internally and through external sources) directly in a web browser without the need for specialized GIS software or large file downloads. HazMapper demonstrates a reproducible, low-friction workflow for sharing large-scale reconnaissance datasets using FAIR principles. Published HazMapper maps containing contextualized geospatial imagery are assigned a persistent, citable URL and accompanying data is published via DesignSafe with a DOI. Additional data collections will be associated with this work later to support longitudinal studies of long-term recovery and resilience related to the LA wildfires. With the existing publications this platform proves an extensible model with clear data provenance for sharing post-disaster geospatial datasets.

session_title: Session 2: Data Foundations: FAIR, Governed, Shared, Verifiable
title: Training Gateways for Responsible AI-Enabled Translational Research: LifeScale, Synthetic Data, GenieAI, and Sandbox-First Hypothesis Registration
speakers: Timothy R. Huerta, Christopher Bartlett
description: **Session Moderator:** Sajida Faiyaz, Austin Community College
abstract: Science gateways have traditionally lowered barriers to advanced computing, data, software, and research infrastructure. In the age of artificial intelligence (AI), the gateway challenge is no longer limited to access. Institutions must also prepare a broader workforce of clinicians, researchers, trainees, data scientists, and informatics professionals to build analytic and AI-enabled workflows responsibly. We describe a training-gateway model built on LifeScale, a governed, multi-institutional Research-Oriented Learning Health System platform at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center and Nationwide Children's Hospital. The model extends LifeScale from a secure data integration platform into a staged workforce development environment that uses synthetic data, AI-assisted development through GenieAI, and sandbox-first analytic workflows to teach practical translational data science. The central design principle is that learners should build, test, and register their hypotheses and code before receiving access to governed research data. Users begin with synthetic datasets, use GenieAI to support natural-language-driven prototyping and code generation, validate their work in a sandbox, register cohort logic and analytic intent, and only then move toward honest-broker-mediated execution against real data. This approach reframes AI-assisted coding from an informal productivity practice into a governed learning pathway with reproducibility, provenance, and data stewardship built in.

session_title: Session 3: AI Inside the Gateway: Agents, Assistants and Guardrails
title: Alexandria: Verification-First Science Gateway for Curating Data from the Scientific Literature
speakers: Priscila Saboia Moreira, Fait Wangui, Don Brower, Andrey Kuehlkamp, Samuel S.C. Rund
description: **Session Moderator:** Ahmad Al-Omari, Our Lady of the Lake University
abstract: Much of the evidence needed for scientific synthesis lives inside figures and tables rather than in the text of a paper, and extracting it into structured, analyzable form is slow, specialized, and labor-intensive work. We present Alexandria, a deployed science gateway that places AI agents alongside the curator rather than in place of the curator: the system reads documents, recognizes figures and tables, digitizes charts, and maps the extracted values onto a curation schema, producing a structured draft in which every value is linked to its source for review and approval. We report on Alexandria's use by biocurators in the VectorByte community, including a hands-on workshop in which 24 participants used the gateway on real papers. A central and initially counterintuitive observation is that the agents make frequent mistakes, yet curators still find the gateway useful: what matters is not the accuracy of the first pass but how cheaply an error can be seen and corrected. By consolidating the paper, its figures, the extracted values, and their provenance in one editable workspace, the gateway turns curation into a review-and-correct task while keeping a human accountable for the record. We reflect on what an agent-assisted, human-in-the-loop approach means for scientific data stewardship, and on extending it beyond a single schema toward cross-domain curation.

session_title: Session 3: AI Inside the Gateway: Agents, Assistants and Guardrails
title: Evaluating Needs in AI-Driven Research: the AI Blueprint Factory
speakers: Jeanette Sperhac, Sean Cleveland
description: **Session Moderator:** Ahmad Al-Omari, Our Lady of the Lake University
abstract: Increasing numbers of academic researchers are turning to AI methods, using its models, algorithms, datasets, and advanced cyberinfrastructure to make fundamental strides in their research. However, academic AI resource availability and adoption lags behind the private sector. The AI Blueprint Factory evaluated the AI needs of research communities that use national-scale computing infrastructure, and made forecasts of needed features and resources. Its study team interviewed scientific researchers across disciplines and seniority levels to determine their perceived research needs and identify opportunities and gaps in AI research support. The focus of this study is evaluating researcher feedback in order to foster the utilization of AI techniques in domain science research. In this paper, we describe the AI Blueprint Factory study and report the challenges and recommendations it identified.

session_title: Session 3: AI Inside the Gateway: Agents, Assistants and Guardrails
title: Integrating AI into a Production Science Gateway: nanoHUB's Path from Curated Content to Actionable Intelligence
speakers: Daniel Mejia, Juan Carlos Verduzco, Alejandro Strachan, Gerhard Klimeck
description: **Session Moderator:** Ahmad Al-Omari, Our Lady of the Lake University
abstract: This work presents nanoHUB as a case study in integrating AI into a production science gateway that has supported research, education, workforce development, online simulation, data, and learning materials for more than two decades. nanoHUB AI combines human-led curation with large language model (LLM)-assisted extraction, validation, and semantic enrichment to transform curated scientific resources into searchable, connected, and reusable knowledge. The system transcribes, summarizes, extracts concepts, indexes resources for semantic search, and organizes relationships in a knowledge graph, while validating model outputs before storage. Models run on Purdue-operated infrastructure so sensitive and unpublished content remains under institutional control. We describe how this architecture supports conversational access, recommendation, MCP-enabled scientific tools, and agent-based workflows for discovery, learning, and scholarly-impact curation in an AI-enabled science gateway.

session_title: Session 3: AI Inside the Gateway: Agents, Assistants and Guardrails
title: A Safety-First Gateway Architecture for Trusted Public Health Resource Navigation
speakers: Jun Zhou, Ben Torkian
description: **Session Moderator:** Ahmad Al-Omari, Our Lady of the Lake University
abstract: Conversational AI can improve access to public health information, but healthcare applications require safe- guards to prevent inappropriate medical guidance and ensure trustworthy responses. We present a Safety-First Science Gateway for maternal and child health (MCH) resource navigation that combines large language models (LLMs) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with a multi-layer safety architecture. The gateway integrates emergency detection, domain validation, citation enforcement, privacy-preserving session manage- ment, and comprehensive audit logging while constraining responses to curated institutional resources. We describe the gateway architecture, implementation, and deployment, emphasizing governance, transparency, and operational readiness rather than unrestricted AI generation. Functional validation demonstrates correct operation of the safety workflows, retrieval pipeline, and monitoring infrastructure. This work provides a reusable architectural framework for deploying trustworthy AI-enabled gateways in public health and other safety-critical domains.

session_title: Session 3: AI Inside the Gateway: Agents, Assistants and Guardrails
title: Gateway-Enabled AlphaFold Workflows for Teaching AI-Driven Structural Biology
speakers: Joseph Tang, Maayan Abudi, Zahara Bobo, Ishaan Chandakkar, Sid Singh, Arunkarthik Vadivelan, Julia Whisler
description: **Session Moderator:** Ahmad Al-Omari, Our Lady of the Lake University
abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming scientific research and creating new opportunities for STEM education. During the 2026 Ohio Supercomputer Center (OSC) STEM Institute, six high school students in this AlphaFold project participated in an 8-day computational biology project designed to introduce protein structure prediction, molecular visualization, and high-performance computing (HPC) concepts using AlphaFold2. Students worked in two teams to investigate biologically significant proteins: the tumor suppressor protein p53 and the SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein. Using AlphaFold-generated structural models, PyMOL visualization, confidence analysis, and structural comparisons with experimentally determined Protein Data Bank (PDB) structures, students explored protein conformations, protein-protein interactions, and the impact of engineered mutations. The p53 team examined monomeric and tetrameric structures and compared AlphaFold-generated conformations with known DNA-bound structures. The Spike protein team investigated differences between wild-type and S2P-stabilized variants used in COVID-19 vaccine development. This project provided students with hands-on experience in AI-enabled scientific workflows while demonstrating how HPC resources support modern biological research. We discuss project outcomes, lessons learned, and the value of integrating AI-driven scientific tools into STEM workforce development programs.

session_title: Session 3: AI Inside the Gateway: Agents, Assistants and Guardrails
title: A Human-Reviewed Science Gateway for AI-Assisted Space Mission Simulation
speakers: Giusy Falcone, Molly Maloney
description: **Session Moderator:** Ahmad Al-Omari, Our Lady of the Lake University
abstract: Space mission simulation is increasingly needed outside the small group of specialists who can install, configure, and maintain astrodynamics software. Students, educators, early mission-design teams, and autonomy researchers often want to ask physically grounded "what if" questions about spacecraft, constellations, environmental perturbations, and mission operations, but the path from intent to executable simulation remains high-friction. Users must translate mission language into model choices, state definitions, force models, output settings, job execution, and validation checks. This barrier limits reuse of simulation infrastructure and makes many early concepts difficult to compare, teach, or scale. This talk presents an early science-gateway architecture for converting space mission intent into executable, human-reviewed SpaceAGORA simulations. SpaceAGORA.jl is an open-source Julia platform for autonomous space systems simulation, with coupled orbit and attitude propagation, multi-agent concepts, environmental perturbation models, and validation against established tools and spacecraft telemetry. The emerging gateway adds a browser-facing layer around this core: user intent is parsed into structured mission descriptions, candidate simulation configurations are generated and schema-checked, jobs are queued to shared compute, SpaceAGORA executes the simulation, and returned artifacts are stored with metadata that records the request, configuration choices, runtime, output volume, validation status, and failure modes. The central design choice is not to remove expert review. Instead, the gateway treats AI assistance as a configuration and explanation layer around a physics-based simulator. Human review remains explicit at the boundary between demonstration, research prototyping, and trusted engineering analysis. This is particularly important for space systems, where plausible-looking visualizations can hide wrong initial conditions, missing force models, misleading output cadence, or inappropriate extrapolation from simplified scenarios. The architecture therefore emphasizes auditable artifacts: generated configuration files, validation summaries, benchmarked reference cases, logs, and reusable campaign metadata. The project is supported by an NSF ACCESS Discover allocation for "Open Space Mission Design and Constellation Simulation Gateway." ACCESS resources will move the computationally meaningful parts of the workflow from lab-PC and small cloud tests to a stable, reviewed environment. Planned workloads include single-spacecraft baselines, simple mission demonstrations, multi-mission scenario families, proliferated-LEO constellation studies, orbit and timing sweeps, environmental-model comparisons, output-cadence studies, and worker-reliability tests. CPU resources generate the SpaceAGORA simulation corpus and benchmark outputs; GPU resources support repeated evaluation of mission-intent translation, configuration generation, validation-support models, result explanation, and retrieval over generated cases; storage preserves reviewed configurations, outputs, logs, and failure cases as reusable mission knowledge. The talk will share the technical architecture, current prototype lessons, and open research questions for gateway builders: how to represent mission intent without erasing domain constraints; how to expose AI-generated configurations without overstating trust; how to make simulation outputs reusable across education and research; and how cyberinfrastructure can lower the barrier to space mission analysis while preserving scientific accountability.

session_title: Session 3: AI Inside the Gateway: Agents, Assistants and Guardrails
title: Coordinating the Multi-Messenger Sky: SCIMMA's HEROIC and Blast in the Age of AI
speakers: Fabián Araneda-Baltierra, Andrew Manning, Gautham Narayan
description: **Session Moderator:** Ahmad Al-Omari, Our Lady of the Lake University
abstract: Multi-messenger astrophysics (MMA) asks scientists to react to fleeting cosmic events, a neutron star merger, a supernova, a high-energy neutrino, within minutes to hours, using facilities that no single institution owns or operates. A gravitational-wave alert, for example, must reach dozens of optical, radio, and high-energy follow-up telescopes, be matched to a location on the sky, and trigger new observations before the transient fades. No individual team can build this pipeline alone; it requires shared cyberinfrastructure that any group in the community can plug into. SCIMMA (Scalable Cyberinfrastructure for Multi-Messenger Astrophysics) exists to be that shared layer, and this talk focuses on two of its production services: HEROIC and Blast. HEROIC is SCIMMA's coordination gateway for MMA follow-up. It serves real-time facility status and lets astronomers submit, track, and manage observing requests across a heterogeneous network of telescopes through one interface, removing the need to learn each facility's own scheduling system. Blast closes the loop after an alert arrives: it ingests live transient streams, associates each transient with its host galaxy, performs multi-wavelength photometry on archival imaging, and infers host properties like stellar mass, star-formation rate, and stellar age, using the Prospector Bayesian inference framework. Full Bayesian SED fitting is normally too slow to keep pace with survey-scale discovery rates, so Blast accelerates it with simulation-based inference (SBI++): a neural network trained on simulated galaxy spectral libraries learns to emulate the posterior directly, cutting inference time from hours to seconds per galaxy without sacrificing accuracy. This is AI embedded not as a demo but as production infrastructure, a direct answer to this year's "Gateways in the Age of AI" theme. Together, HEROIC and Blast show two complementary ways gateways can absorb complexity for a time-pressured community: one orchestrating human and facility coordination, the other automating a computationally expensive inference step. Both sit on shared SCIMMA foundations, including Hopskotch, a Kafka-based low-latency alert messaging and archive system, and federated identity and access management, so authentication, alert distribution, and data provenance are solved once and reused across services rather than rebuilt per tool. MMA has produced some of the most publicly visible results in physics this decade, from the first neutron star merger detection to ongoing gravitational-wave and electromagnetic joint campaigns, giving this work a natural audience beyond the gateways community. Blast has been running continuously since mid-2024, ingesting alerts from the Transient Name Server and producing host-galaxy characterizations for thousands of transients to date, with a worker-queue architecture designed to scale toward the far higher alert volumes expected from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Both services are open source, expose public APIs alongside their browser interfaces, and are built by a distributed team of research software engineers explicitly to be reusable outside SCIMMA's home institutions, a design choice motivated as much by long-term sustainability as by access. This talk will cover the architecture of both services, current adoption and operational results, and lessons learned in building AI-enabled, community-operated infrastructure for a domain where speed is scientifically non-negotiable.

session_title: Session 4: Readiness for the AI Age: Learning, Workforce and Community
title: AI Readiness as a Community Accomplishment: Communities of Practice and Sustainable Science Gateways
speakers: Mahedi Hasan, Kerk F Kee, Ewa Deelman, Melissa Santillana, Kulsawasd Jitkajornwanich, Jon McNaughtan
description: **Session Moderator:** Drew LaMar, College of William and Mary
abstract: Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork and 26 semi-structured interviews from a qualitative study of cyberinfrastructure adoption in scientific organizations closely related to science gateways, this paper argues that AI readiness is produced in community through shared practices, trust relations, and learning processes that sustain shared cyberinfrastructure over time. This paper integrates Diffusion of Innovations theory with the Communities of Practice framework to show that adoption attributes such as compatibility, trialability, and observability are socially produced through community interaction rather than individual judgment alone. Across the interviews, three patterns emerge: AI readiness is co-defined rather than prescribed, adoption travels on trust and small-scale trial, and readiness is rehearsed and distributed through training and participation. Although the empirical material comes from a research vessel and related cyberinfrastructure settings rather than science gateways directly, these mechanisms are likely to extend to gateway communities because gateways must also absorb new sociotechnical risk through shared governance, trust-building, and distributed learning.

session_title: Session 4: Readiness for the AI Age: Learning, Workforce and Community
title: A Wiki-Grounded Educational Gateway for Course-Aware Socratic LLM Tutoring: Built on the llm-wiki Pattern
speakers: Priscila Saboia Moreira, Charles Vardeman II, Christopher R. Sweet
description: **Session Moderator:** Drew LaMar, College of William and Mary
abstract: Generic large language model chatbots have become the default interface undergraduates reach for when completing laboratory assignments. They answer well and quickly, and in doing so they collapse the reasoning path the assignment was designed to elicit. Retrieval-augmented generation over the course materials does not fix this: the tutor still delivers the answer, only now with citations attached. Rather than changing how documents are retrieved, we change how the student interacts with the model, and we package that change as a small, forkable educational gateway. The gateway couples two artifacts. A course-specific wiki, maintained under the llm-wiki pattern, provides an instructor-curated knowledge base. A Socratic dialogue policy forbids answer delivery and requires every response to visibly cite the wiki. Because both the course knowledge, held as an LLM-maintained wiki memory, and the tutoring policy are specified in these artifacts rather than in the model, the tutor launches with one command from a fresh clone once model access is provisioned, and a new curriculum drops into the same template by swapping the wiki. The instantiation reported here is scoped to the Purdue SCALE Introduction to Engineering with Microelectronics curriculum on the Arduino UNO. A worked scenario, authored by us, illustrates the interaction the design is meant to produce: on a diagnostic follow-up about forward voltage, the tutored student has a derivation and cited wiki pages to return to. We tested the refuse-to-answer policy with 225 scripted adversarial sessions across three models, spanning direct demands, fabricated authority, prompt injection, and multi-turn escalation. The policy gave way in six incremental-extraction sessions and held in the rest.

session_title: Session 4: Readiness for the AI Age: Learning, Workforce and Community
title: From Access to Understanding: The GATE Framework for Science Gateway Learning and Responsible AI Use in Community College Cybersecurity Education
speakers: Kristine Christensen, S.Charlie Dey
description: **Session Moderator:** Drew LaMar, College of William and Mary
abstract: Science gateways can give community college students earlier access to high-performance computing, data, software, models, instruments, and research workflows that are difficult to reproduce in many teaching environments. These tools can make research infrastructure more visible and approachable, especially when students work with real-world or realistic data sets connected to problems they recognize. Yet access alone does not produce understanding. Students need time to learn what gateway resources are, how they work, why datasets and assumptions matter, and how outputs should be interpreted before artificial intelligence is introduced as a learning support. This paper presents GATE, or Gateway Access, Teaching, and Ethics, as a scaffolded framework for community college science gateway learning. The framework uses Bloom's Taxonomy to organize learning progression and the AI Assessment Scale to guide when and how AI should be limited, guided, or expanded. GATE emphasizes building foundational skill development, hands-on engagement with relevant datasets, ethical reasoning, human judgment, and the productive friction students need to build confidence and durable understanding. A cybersecurity phishing-detection use case illustrates how students can use gateway resources to explore data, models, computational workflows, and responsible AI practices without bypassing the cognitive work that makes learning meaningful. The framework supports expanded access, accessibility, reproducibility, and sustainable instructional design for gateway-powered education. For the gateways community, GATE offers a reusable model for moving new learners from gateway access to meaningful, ethical, and reproducible use of gateway-enabled resources.

session_title: Session 4: Readiness for the AI Age: Learning, Workforce and Community
title: Teaching Advanced Data Science and Gateway Development Through Guided Codeathons: Prompt-Augmented Learning with Real World Data
speakers: Charlie Dey, Je'Aime Powell, Linda Hayden
description: **Session Moderator:** Drew LaMar, College of William and Mary
abstract: Building proficiency in advanced data science and research computing requires exposure to complex, real‑world datasets. Unfortunately, real-world datasets often present major obstacles to building the necessary context and understanding for novice learners. By blending the urgency of an educational hackathon with the structure and scaffolding of a laboratory experiment, we developed a guided "codeathon" designed to teach practical advanced computing concepts. Built around the Robbins (2018) lunar crater database, the curriculum emphasizes data exploration, transformation, visualization, and gateway interface prototyping. A key contribution of this codeathon was the integration of prompt engineering, enabling students to build context around the dataset, construct code, interpret outputs, and generate interfaces through natural language interaction with AI tools. Observations from the event suggest that this approach dramatically reduced syntactic barriers while preserving analytical understanding and accuracy, allowing students to engage earlier with higher‑order data science practices. This 90-minute community coding experience was showcased during the ADMI 2026 symposium with approximately 55 undergraduate students from Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) and Minority Serving Institutions (MSIs). We discuss the instructional design, learning outcomes, and implications for research computing education, arguing that prompt‑augmented workflows represent a critical evolution in how we train the next generation of gateway developers and computational scientists.

session_title: Session 4: Readiness for the AI Age: Learning, Workforce and Community
title: Helping Research Software Engineers Craft Better Prompts for Requirement Engineering Tasks
speakers: Minhyuk Ko, Yoseph Berhanu Alebachew, Rayn Owens, Chris Brown
description: **Session Moderator:** Drew LaMar, College of William and Mary
abstract: Research Software Engineers (RSEs) combine expertise in programming with an understanding of research to advance scientific discovery. Studies show 92% of researchers use software in their research and 56% report developing their own software. Despite this, most RSEs lack formal training in software engineering (SE) concepts, such as requirements engineering (RE), or the process of identifying and assessing the needs that a system is to fulfill. However, existing SE research and development tools often fail to address the unique needs of RSEs, who operate at the intersection of scientific discovery and programming, rather than within the constraints of a traditional software development role. Furthermore, views of RSEs have been underrepresented by the scientific community. RE for research software requires different software development techniques, and is often ignored by RSEs. For instance, prior work shows RSEs struggle with RE as they often develop software in an ad hoc manner without following stringent processes. Furthermore, RSEs are less likely to adopt state-of-the-art software development tools, such as Git. Recently, large language models (LLMs) — generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools trained on vast amounts of data and code — have transformed SE. For instance, prior work demonstrates LLMs are capable of supporting RE tasks. LLMs are also increasingly used to develop research software. Our prior work has found that RSEs desire AI tools and features to overcome challenges in research software development. However, effectively utilizing LLMs, especially in SE tasks, heavily depends on prompting — natural-language instructions given to LLMs. Prompt formatting has a significant impact on LLM performance, and is critical for RE tasks with LLMs. However, research shows non-experts struggle to craft effective prompts, frequently failing to iterate systematically or align prompts with the model’s capabilities. Software practitioners also report prompt engineering is a key challenge in interactions with LLMs, motivating the need for novel SE and research software engineering prompt crafting approaches. To democratize prompt engineering among RSEs, we introduce PromptRSE, a tool designed to help RSEs craft effective prompts that enable LLMs to generate contextually tailored responses for their research software development tasks. In the current prototype implementation, PromptRSE incorporates empirically grounded guidelines for prompting LLMs during RE activities. The tool provides feedback on prompt formulation, assisting users in refining their inputs to obtain results that better align with their intended goals. Through a preliminary user study, we investigate the following research questions: - How do RSEs’ preferences differ between PromptRSE-generated prompts and original user prompts? - How do RSEs perceive the usability, ease of use, and usefulness of PromptRSE? We conducted a chatbot arena study, where 17 RSEs from diverse fields used PromptRSE to complete research SE tasks in their respective domains. We found participants preferred responses to prompts generated by PromptRSE, and post-survey results showed the tool was usable and easy to use, with participants expressing willingness to adopt it into their workflows. Based on our findings, we provide implications for future tools and techniques to enhance LLM-assisted SE for programmers from diverse disciplines.

session_title: Session 4: Readiness for the AI Age: Learning, Workforce and Community
title: Is Your Science Gateway Ready for the AI Age? Communication Strategies for Sustainable Adoption and Diffusion for Science Gateways
speakers: Md Ashraful Goni, Kulsawasd Jitkajornwanich, Prasad Calyam, Kerk F. Kee
description: **Session Moderator:** Drew LaMar, College of William and Mary
abstract: Is your science gateway ready for the AI age? As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes embedded in science gateway architectures through conversational chatbots, AI-ranked search results, and large language model interfaces, gateway teams face a new and urgent question: not only whether their platforms are technically capable of integrating AI, but whether their communication strategies are ready to support sustainable adoption of AI-powered features. Drawing on four studies conducted with the KnowCOVID-19 science gateway, including qualitative interviews with medical professionals, a conceptual inquiry into AI as a gateway, survey-based competence metrics, and user imagination research, this paper argues that the adoption challenges identified in the pre-AI era are not resolved by AI integration but are instead amplified. We revisit and extend Kee et al.'s seven external communication strategies for science gateway diffusion in light of AI-specific adoption barriers, including trust in AI-generated outputs, user competence variation, and the tension between conversational interfaces and scientific accountability. We propose an updated communication framework with AI-era extensions for each strategy. Implications are offered for gateway developers, outreach educators, and science gateway funders seeking to assess and strengthen their communication readiness for the AI era.
